title: Online Tutoring
subtitle: Turn what you know into a clear learning result—not a 60-minute screen share with excellent intentions

blocks.text: Knowing algebra and teaching algebra are cousins, not twins. One solves for x; the other calmly explains why x keeps leaving the house without telling anyone.

Online tutoring is a service business built around a specific learner, subject and measurable outcome. A strong tutor does not promise guaranteed grades. They assess the starting point, teach a focused skill, check understanding and communicate progress. When working with minors, the tutor also needs parent or guardian consent, safe communication rules and privacy-conscious technology.
A narrow offer is easier to sell and deliver: for example, Grade 9 Ontario math problem solving or CELPIP speaking feedback—not “all subjects, all ages, all planets.”

items.title: Choose a learner, subject and outcome.
Set pricing, policies and progress measures.
Protect student privacy and copyrighted material.
Complete a First Student Learning Studio Plan.
“A tutor must know every answer immediately.”
items.text: A credible tutor can pause, verify and model how to find an answer. Confidently inventing a formula is performance art, not instruction.

sections.title: Sell Progress That Can Be Observed

blocks.text: A tutoring offer becomes sellable the moment progress can be shown, not just felt.

items.title: LEARNER
items.text: Choose an age group, curriculum, exam, language level or professional skill you can support accurately.

items.title: STARTING POINT
items.text: Use a short diagnostic, sample work and learner conversation. Do not turn the first meeting into an ambush exam with dramatic music.

items.title: OUTCOME
items.text: Describe what the learner should be able to do: solve a type of problem, organize an essay, explain a concept or improve a practice score.

items.title: EVIDENCE
items.text: Compare attempts, error patterns, completed practice and learner explanations. Grades may matter, but they are affected by more than tutoring.

blocks.text: A useful 60-minute session can follow five moves: check-in, retrieve prior learning, model one skill, practise with feedback and assign a small next step.
For minors, keep parent or guardian consent, scheduling and payment in an adult-controlled channel. Agree on recording, messaging, missed sessions and who receives progress updates.

items.title: “More worksheets automatically create more learning.”
items.text: Practice helps when it targets the learner's actual error and includes feedback. A 42-page packet can also become a very effective coaster.

sections.title: Build the Business Around the Lesson

blocks.text: Price the complete service: planning, delivery, feedback, platform fees, payment processing, materials, bookkeeping, cancellations and communication.

Tutoring that follows a provincial curriculum, supports certain credit courses or meets specified prerequisite rules may be GST/HST-exempt. Other instruction may be taxable; the label “tutor” does not decide the answer.
The $30,000 small-supplier threshold applies to taxable supplies, not automatically to exempt tutoring revenue. Classify the service before using the threshold.

items.title: “All tutoring is automatically GST/HST-exempt.”
items.text: The exemption depends on what is taught and how it connects to a designated curriculum, credit course or qualifying prerequisite. Verify the actual supply.

blocks.text: Key takeaway: A tutoring business earns trust by narrowing the offer, diagnosing before teaching, measuring one clear learning result, protecting young learners and operating with written pricing, privacy, copyright and cancellation rules.

sections.title: Eli Teaches Less and Learns More

paragraphs: Eli Tremblay began tutoring high-school math online from Moncton. His first advertisement offered calculus, chemistry, essay writing and “general academic confidence.” It sounded impressive and slightly like four businesses sharing one trench coat.

The conflict arrived during a Grade 9 session. Eli had prepared advanced equations, but his learner, Sophie, was losing marks because she skipped signs when moving terms. More content would not solve a smaller, repeatable error.

Eli used three sample problems, asked Sophie to explain each step and built a one-page sign-check routine. He sent her parent a brief progress note, scheduled two focused sessions and rewrote his offer around Grade 9 and 10 math problem solving.
Sophie became more accurate, and Eli gained a service he could explain, repeat and improve. His new slogan was not literally “fewer subjects, fewer trench coats,” but the principle remained sound.

blocks.text: The first session should produce a small win and a next-step diagnosis. A learner who understands the plan is more likely to practise between sessions.
A narrower offer diagnosed the real error instead of adding more content on top of it.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: Why is a narrow tutoring offer easier to operate?
items.detail: It is easier to sell and deliver because the tutor can accurately support one age group, curriculum, exam or skill instead of promising every subject to every learner.

items.title: What should happen before a tutor chooses the lesson?
items.detail: A short diagnostic, sample work and learner conversation to establish the starting point.

items.title: Why should grades not be guaranteed?
items.detail: Grades are evidence of progress but are affected by more than tutoring, so outcomes should describe an observable skill instead.

items.title: What privacy controls matter when tutoring a minor?
items.detail: Parent or guardian consent, scheduling and payment kept in an adult-controlled channel, plus agreed rules on recording, messaging and progress updates.

items.title: Why must GST/HST treatment be checked rather than assumed?
items.detail: The exemption depends on what is taught and how it connects to a designated curriculum, credit course or qualifying prerequisite—not the label “tutor.”

sections.title: Your Action: Complete Your First Student Learning Studio Plan

blocks.text: Use general learner descriptions. Do not record a child’s full name, school login, birth date, private assessment or meeting password on this worksheet.

Keep progress notes short and useful: skill attempted, evidence observed, feedback given and next step. First-offer test: explain the learner, problem, outcome, session format and price in two sentences.

items.title: Diagnostic
items.text: Short assessment used to identify a learner's starting point.

items.title: Learning outcome
items.text: Specific ability the learner should demonstrate.

items.title: Session arc
items.text: Repeatable sequence used to structure a lesson.

items.title: Retrieval practice
items.text: Recalling prior learning without first reviewing the answer.

items.title: Progress note
items.text: Brief record of evidence, feedback and next step.

items.title: Exempt supply
items.text: Service on which GST/HST is generally not charged.

items.title: CASL
items.text: Canadian rules governing commercial electronic messages.
